messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Nurse
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 68

He is a 44-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working as a nurse, someone other people describe as steady-handed and dependable. In the hospital, he is the one who notices when a patient is getting worse before the monitor changes, the one who speaks gently to frightened families, the one newer staff turn to when a shift becomes chaotic. At home, before the robbery, his wife knows him as practical and quiet, a man who unwinds by making tea late at night after work and checking that the doors are locked only once before bed.

The robbery happens on an ordinary evening after a long shift. He leaves the hospital tired, still carrying the clipped, alert energy of work. He stops at a convenience store on his way home to pick up bread and milk. In the parking lot, as he reaches his car, two men approach him fast. At first he thinks they are asking for directions. Then one of them steps close, demands his wallet, and shoves him hard against the side of the car. He remembers the cold shock of metal at his ribs, though even now he is not sure whether it is a knife or only something meant to feel like one. What stays with him is the smell of sweat, the pressure in his chest, and the sudden certainty that he might die there in his scrubs with his hospital ID still hanging from his pocket. He hands over his wallet and phone, but one man strikes him across the face anyway. He hears himself apologizing, as if he has done something wrong. After they run, he stands frozen in the lot, unable to bend down to pick up the groceries that have spilled onto the pavement.

In the first days afterward, he tells himself he is lucky. He is not stabbed, not shot, not hospitalized. He returns to work quickly, embarrassed by how shaken he feels by “just a robbery.” But his body does not seem to believe the event is over. In the emergency department, when voices rise suddenly behind him, he flinches so sharply that a coworker jokes about him being jumpy. The sliding doors opening at night make his heart race. Every man in a hooded sweatshirt catches his eye. He starts scanning hands, waistbands, exits. He tells himself this is sensible, but it is exhausting.

Sleep changes first and then everything else begins to organize itself around that. He falls asleep late and wakes abruptly, heart hammering, after dreams in which he cannot move or cannot speak. Sometimes he is back in the parking lot; other times the scene is distorted, with one of his patients lying where he had been standing, helpless and exposed. His wife wakes to find him sitting on the edge of the bed listening for sounds outside. He begins checking the locks repeatedly, then checking the windows, then standing in the dark living room looking out between the curtains. If she asks what he is doing, he says, “Nothing, just making sure.”

He avoids the parking lot where it happened, then the whole shopping area, then any errand after dark. If his wife asks him to stop for groceries after work, he makes an excuse. He takes longer routes home to avoid that street. At the hospital, he volunteers for tasks that keep him inside and asks coworkers to walk with him to the staff lot after evening shifts, though he is ashamed of needing that. He used to pride himself on calming distressed patients, but now when agitated men come into the unit, especially if they are intoxicated or demanding, he feels heat rise in his body and has to work to keep his voice even. Once, when a patient grabs at his sleeve, he jerks away so forcefully that the patient stares at him. For the rest of the shift he is flooded with guilt and keeps replaying it, hearing again the robber’s voice, feeling again that pinned, trapped sensation.

At home he becomes more distant than he means to be. His wife says he is physically present but never fully settles. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants and grows irritated if she lingers in a parking lot or talks on her phone while walking to the car. He snaps at small things and then feels ashamed. On weekends, when family invites them to gatherings, he often refuses, saying he is tired from work. The truth is that crowds make him feel exposed, and he no longer trusts the ordinary ease other people seem to move through the world with. He misses the version of himself who could.

What troubles him almost as much as the fear is the way the robbery has changed his understanding of himself. As a nurse, he is used to being the competent one in emergencies. He has helped restrain combative patients, started CPR, spoken to families after devastating news. He cannot reconcile that identity with the memory of apologizing to the men who robbed him, with the fact that he froze. He knows professionally that fear can overtake anyone, that survival is not cowardice, yet he cannot extend that same compassion to himself.

Months later, he still measures his days around the possibility of danger. He keeps seeing the parking lot in flashes: the spilled milk rolling away, the scrape of his shoulder against the car door, the sound of footsteps running off. He feels older now, more brittle. He goes to work, pays the bills, speaks gently to patients, and tries to look unchanged. But inside, he moves through the world as if something violent could break through at any moment, and some part of him remains in that parking lot, waiting for the next blow.
